lead: Seamanship is choosing the method before you start: which knot, how much chain, which line first, which sail. The load, the wind and the stream decide.

head: Knot
Job
rows: Loop for a bollard; never jams
Two loops: a sling for a person
Round turn and two half hitches
To a ring; freed under load
Grips a loaded line or chain

blocks.p: One locking hitch on a cleat: more jam. Clear a **riding turn** by taking the load on a rolling hitch led to another winch. Put three turns on the winch before opening a loaded clutch, and ease with a flat palm, never with the tail round your hand.

fig.note: Lead from just below the drum: no riding turns

blocks.p: **Nylon** stretches, for warps and mooring lines; a halyard must not; a painter should float. Splice a permanent eye, whip a cut end, coil braid in figure-of-eights. In a surge add chafe guards, doubled lines and snubbers. Lash deck gear with several turns to strong points, frapped tight.

fig.note: Throwing upwind: end fast, coil split, aim past him

sections.title: Scope from the bow roller, at high water

blocks.p: Anchor for the **forecast** wind: if a shift will make the bay a lee shore, move in daylight. Choose sand, enough water at low water, and neighbours on your kind of rode: rope boats range wider than chain boats, moored boats hardly move.

fig.note: On all chain, anchor at A: they swing as you do

blocks.p: **Scope** is rode against high-water depth plus bow-roller height: 4:1 on chain, 5:1 before a blow, 6:1 on rope.

fig.title: (3.0 + 3.6 + 1.0) × 4 ≈ 30 m
lines: LW + 2 h, range 4.8 m
Risen 3/12: 1.2 m
Still to come: 3.6 m

blocks.p: Approach head to wind and let go as she gathers sternway, so the chain lays out in a line; under sail, come in under main alone. Go astern firmly and watch a **transit abeam**: if it stays closed, she holds.

fig.title: Swinging room and anchor alarm
lines: 35 m of chain · depth 5 m + roller 1 m
Along the bottom: √(35² − 6²) ≈ 34 m
Plus 12 m of boat: she reaches 46 m
A rock 40 m from the anchor is too close
Alarm: centred on the anchor, not the boat

blocks.p: In a rising wind set **anchor watches** with written orders: call the skipper if a bearing shifts, the wind passes a set force or a boat drags nearby.

fig.title: Dragging
lines: Engine on first: you keep control
Motor up to ease the load
Re-anchor with more scope, or move
Fails again, lee shore astern: out to sea
A boat dragging onto you: fenders out,
horn and torch to wake her crew

head: Problem
Answer
rows: Bahamian moor: anchors up and downstream
Tandem: kedge ahead, chained to the bower's crown
Tripping line from crown to buoy
Chain cleated short; motor the opposite way
Hold it on a line, lower yours clear

fig.title: Tripping line: about 8 m
lines: Low water, range 2.5 m
HW depth 4.0 + 2.5 = 6.5 m
A little more than that

fig.note: Kedge laid astern by dinghy: haul off as she lifts

blocks.p: To weigh, motor gently up the chain as the bow crew points: the windlass only lifts.

sections.title: Prop walk and the pivot point
refs: Boat handling — turning in a tight space

blocks.p: Astern, a **right-handed** propeller kicks the stern to port, most strongly from rest; a left-handed one, to starboard. The wash boils up on the side opposite the kick. So berth port side to, where braking pulls the stern in, and turn short round to starboard.

fig.note: Astern from rest · right-handed prop: stern to port

blocks.p: Ahead, she pivots a third of her length from the bow and the stern swings out, towards the quay you are leaving. Astern, the pivot moves aft and the **bow** sweeps wide.
Approach a berth or buoy into whichever is stronger, wind or stream, as the moored boats lie. To **ferry glide**, stem the stream at its own speed with the bow angled slightly in.

fig.note: Stem the stream at 2 kn, bow a little in: she crabs across

fig.title: Catamaran: two engines far apart
lines: One ahead, one astern: she spins on the spot,
towards the engine going astern
Bows blow off: leeward ahead, windward astern
Pinned on: bow spring, outboard engine ahead
Tacking: jib aback until the bows are through
At anchor: a bridle from both bows

head: Situation
Method
rows: Stop parallel, a beam off; she blows in
Steeper, with way; midships line first, then ahead on it
Ahead on the bow spring; stern out, then astern
Stern spring only: the stream pushes the bow out
Aim to windward; windward lines first on, last off
Own shore lines, masts staggered; from inside, leave down-tide

blocks.p: Stern-to on your own anchor, let go a little upwind; if the bow sags downwind later, tighten the chain.

fig.title: Lazy-line berth
lines: In: windward stern line first
Lazy line to the bow, outside everything
Haul it taut, cleat it at the bow
Out: drop the lazy line, let it sink,
then slip the stern lines and go

blocks.p: On a buoy lie to a **slip line** through the ring, both ends aboard. If the boat hook is being dragged away, let it go and come round again.
**Heave to**: tack with the jib sheet left made fast, ease the main, lash the tiller to leeward. She still drifts: 4 h at 1.2 kn is 4.8 M.

fig.note: Hove to on port tack: jib aback, tiller to leeward

fig.title: Slab reef
lines: Reef early · at night before it is urgent
Everyone clipped on, the main eased
1  Ease the kicker and the mainsheet
2  Lower the halyard, hook on the tack
3  Re-hoist, then haul in the reef line
Genoa: roll it against a little sheet tension

blocks.p: Heavy **weather helm** is too much main and heel: ease the traveller, then reef. Lee helm is too much sail forward: roll some genoa. Beating into a steep sea, steer a little free, luff up the face, bear away over the crest.

fig.note: Wind and boom on the same side

blocks.p: Use the sail you can spill: head to wind, the main; stemming a tide with the wind astern, at a mooring, the **jib alone**. To sail off an anchor, back the jib to port and the bow pays off to starboard.

sections.title: Stretch, a bridle and low speed

blocks.p: Tow on **nylon**, the anchor warp, from a **bridle**: both bow cleats through the bow roller on the casualty, both quarters on the tug, so she can still steer. Windlass and pulpit are not built for it.

fig.note: A bridle at each end keeps the pull central

fig.title: Towing a 10 m yacht
lines: Crests 20 m apart: towline 40 m, two waves
Hull speed 7 kn: tow at 5 kn
Long tow: more line, a weight in the middle,
a chafe guard at the fairlead
In harbour: alongside, your stern aft of hers

blocks.p: Tow the dinghy with the outboard aboard, on two painters, on the back of a following wave; tie her short alongside before you reverse. Ashore at night: two trips, lifejackets, kill cord, torch.
